keyPoints: Artificial Intelligence is the broad goal of building machines that exhibit intelligent behavior.
Machine Learning is a subset of AI: a set of techniques that let systems learn patterns from data rather than being explicitly programmed.

Data Science is the broader discipline that supplies, cleans and analyzes the data ML algorithms are trained on, and applies statistical/ML techniques (including AI methods) to draw insights and support decisions.
In practice the three overlap heavily: data science provides the data pipeline, machine learning provides the modelling technique, and AI is the umbrella goal both work toward.
modelAnswer: Artificial Intelligence is the broad field of creating intelligent systems. Machine Learning is a subset of AI that uses algorithms and statistical modelling to learn patterns from data. Data Science is an interdisciplinary field of mathematics, statistics and computer science that extracts meaningful insights and supports informed decisions. The fields overlap because they all use data, algorithms and models: Data Science supplies and analyses data, Machine Learning learns patterns and produces predictions or classifications, and AI applies such methods to create systems that show intelligent behaviour and automate tasks.

stem: Which of the following best explains the purpose of a histogram?

keyPoints: Bar chart: compares quantities across categories, e.g. sales by region.
Line chart: shows a trend over time, e.g. monthly website traffic.
Pie chart: shows proportions of a whole, e.g. market share by company.
(A fourth common type, scatter plot, shows the relationship between two numeric variables, e.g. study hours vs exam score, and may be offered as an alternative.)
modelAnswer: A bar chart compares quantities across categories, such as students' marks in different subjects or sales of different products. A line chart shows how values change over time, such as monthly sales or website traffic. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, such as the market share of different companies.
stem: Identify any three types of data visualization, give their applications as well.

keyPoints: Visualizations can show a range rather than a single value to convey uncertainty, e.g. error bars on a bar/line chart showing the margin of error around a measured value.
A shaded confidence-interval band around a forecast line (e.g. a weather forecast's temperature range for the coming days) visually communicates how confident the prediction is.
Both techniques let a viewer judge how much to trust a given data point, rather than presenting it as an exact certainty.
stem: Discuss the way data visualization can be used to communicate data uncertainty, provide two specific examples.

keyPoints: Consider the data type: categorical data suits bar/pie charts, continuous/time-series data suits line charts, and relationships between two numeric variables suit scatter plots.
Consider the message: comparison, trend, distribution, or composition each has a chart type that communicates it most clearly.
Consider the audience: a simpler chart (bar/pie) suits a general audience, while a technical audience may benefit from a more detailed chart (box plot, scatter with regression line).
Avoid distortion (e.g. truncated axes, 3D effects) that could visually mislead the viewer about the data.
modelAnswer: Choose a visualization according to the data and the message it must communicate. Numerical data can use quantitative charts, categorical data can use bar or pie charts, and data changing over time can use a line graph. Relationships among several numerical variables can use scatter plots or heatmaps. The chart should make the intended comparison, trend, distribution or composition clear to its audience without distorting the data.
stem: Describe the key considerations in selecting appropriate visualizations for different types of data and analyses?

keyPoints: Data visualization makes large or complex datasets easier to understand at a glance by turning numbers into visual patterns.
It helps identify trends, outliers and correlations that would be hard to spot in a raw table.
It supports communication and decision-making, letting non-technical stakeholders quickly grasp findings and act on them.
It is used across fields: business dashboards for KPIs, scientific research for presenting results, journalism for data storytelling, and public health for tracking disease spread.
modelAnswer: Data visualization turns data into charts, graphs and maps so complex information is easier to understand and can support meaningful decisions. It helps people identify trends, patterns and useful information, and it communicates findings to non-technical stakeholders. In business intelligence it reveals market trends and tracks performance; in education it supports data literacy, concept building and critical thinking; and in science and daily life it helps people interpret and use data.
stem: Explain the uses of data visualization in detail.

keyPoints: Poor-quality data (missing values, errors, duplicates, bias) leads a model to learn incorrect or misleading patterns.
This results in inaccurate predictions and lower model accuracy/reliability.
It can introduce or amplify bias, causing the model to perform unfairly for some groups.
It can also cause the model to fail unexpectedly in production, requiring costly retraining or redesign, and undermines trust in the model's outputs.
modelAnswer: Poor data quality, such as missing values, errors or duplicate records, can cause a model to learn incorrect patterns. Its predictions then become inaccurate and less reliable. Poor-quality or biased data can also make results unfair for some groups, and failures after deployment may require retraining or redesign. Because the quality of collected data directly affects later results, it also reduces confidence in the model's outputs.
stem: What are the potential consequences of poor data quality on model performance?
